problem: SLAM-based metric-semantic maps break under appearance change and dynamics because relocalization and data association fail. Sparse topological graphs with VPR suffer perceptual aliasing and a precision-recall trade-off in loop closure and relocalization.
motivation: Robots need to reuse a single spatial-semantic memory over long-term operation despite lighting, seasonal and object-arrangement change. Committing to a single VPR match risks false relocalization, while conservative thresholds miss relocalization under severe change. Explicit reasoning over ambiguity with motion cues can resolve this.
key_idea: Replace the metric SLAM substrate with an online pose-aware topological graph of RGB-D keyframes and relocalize via sequential hypothesis testing over a bounded Gaussian-mixture belief in continuous SE(3), using a global VPR+PnP measurement message.
insight: Keeping multiple continuous SE(3) pose hypotheses and confirming them over time with motion cues lets the system accept VPR matches safely. Loop closures and kidnapped-robot events become hypothesis births and merges. The comparison against PBU (the discrete-state analogue of SHT) shows continuous-state filtering gives higher relocalization success, and on Topo-Bench the largest gain is in the aliased A+P regime. Replacing PnP with VGGT gives 0% success because of inconsistent scale, and it runs about 30x slower (490 ms vs 16 ms).
method: Pose-aware topological graph: nodes store RGB-D keyframes and SE(3) Gaussian-mixture poses; odometry edges and proximity edges (d=0.5 m); a new node is created when the max VPR similarity falls below a threshold β.
Motion message: each SE(3) mixture component is pushed forward with odometry via adjoint covariance transport plus process noise, and weights are preserved.

Global measurement message: BoQ VPR retrieves keyframes, and XFeat+LightGlue+E-PnP RANSAC gives relative poses. Association probability P(i)=softmax(π(i)·inlier(i)/M) forms a mixture over all retrieved keyframes, so it can handle loop closure and kidnapping.

Hypothesis management: SE(3)-aware DBSCAN clustering of measurement components (top K=5), fusion with motion components via Gaussian product and overlap weight, pruning of low-weight components, and birth of new hypotheses via a restart switch.
Per-hypothesis smoothing: pose-graph optimization with GTSAM over odometry and visual constraints, run independently per hypothesis.
Loop closure by SHT: accumulate log posterior odds vs the tracked hypothesis over a sliding window W (count>r), then run a joint PGO and merge the hypotheses.

setting.backbone: BoQ (VPR) + XFeat + LightGlue + E-PnP, with a Gaussian-mixture filter (all off-the-shelf, frozen)
setting.training_data: none (uses pretrained VPR/feature models, no new training)
setting.action_space: Not applicable for the mapping/localization module; on the robot, local obstacle avoidance and relative waypoint tracking
setting.simulator: real-world datasets (OpenLORIS, Rover, Topo-Bench) plus real quadruped robot
setting.privileged: none (odometry input; GT used only for evaluation)

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks, not canonical ones. Noisy-odometry, fast-motion and occlusion results are qualitative only. Runtime (~28 ms/step) is reported.
results: CROSS achieves the best relocalization success across sequences (0.384 overall vs RTAB-Map 0.198, the best baseline, in cross-sequence). With self mapping it reaches 0.488 vs 0.387 for SM. On Topo-Bench it gets the best BLA (0.452 vs RTAB-Map 0.301). In real-robot ObjectNav it reaches 70/80/80% vs 40/60/30% for the best baseline (RTAB-Map).
limitations: Absolute cross-sequence success is still only ~40% under severe shifts such as day-to-night or seasonal change.
The classical keypoint+PnP relative pose front-end is a bottleneck under severe appearance change and noisy depth, which can create wrong measurement modes.
The real-robot evaluation is small (10 trials per setting); the baselines are reimplemented and the topological baselines are simple.
